articles.title_orig: One passport isn’t enough for some wealthy Chinese. Here’s where they’re looking next
articles.title_zh: One passport isn’t enough for some wealthy Chinese. Here’s where they’re looking next
articles.content_orig:
For some wealthy Chinese, securing a foreign passport is becoming the ultimate trade-off: giving up their Chinese citizenship.
Wealth advisors say a growing number of affluent Chinese are considering renouncing their nationality as Beijing intensifies scrutiny of offshore wealth, with concerns over taxes, geopolitical uncertainty and greater international mobility driving their interest in alternative passports.
China does not recognize dual nationality, meaning Chinese nationals seeking to acquire foreign citizenship must renounce their passports.
"We have had some clients who are willing to give up their Chinese citizenship to hold multiple passports," said Armand Arton, CEO of immigration migration consultancy Arton Capital, who added that the choice of passports depends on their lifestyle and business needs.
Meanwhile, Ryan Lin, director at Singapore-based legal firm Bayfront Law, said he has seen an increase in wealthy Chinese considering renouncing their nationality since July.
That month, Beijing introduced new measures targeting offshore trusts, with certain incomes and transactions potentially subject to a 20% tax. The changes have prompted some families to reassess how they hold and transfer assets overseas.
Previously, clients would discuss the possibility of giving up their citizenship. Now, more are expressing concrete intentions to do so, Lin told CNBC.
Manish Tibrewal, co-founder of multi-family office Farro Capital, also reported growing interest in foreign passports.
The wealth advisory firm is helping some Chinese families pursue Caribbean citizenship alongside Singapore permanent residency, with the longer-term possibility of obtaining Singapore citizenship, subject to government approval.
Tibrewal said the number of Chinese families actively exploring alternative citizenship options since July far exceeds those who have completed the process last year.
Inquiries from Chinese clients have risen 33% since July, investment migration firm Savory & Partners said, while Global Citizen Solutions reported an increase of nearly 40% compared with the same period last year.
Both firms specialize in investment migration, which helps wealthy individuals obtain foreign residency or citizenship, often through qualifying investments in their destination countries.
Renouncing Chinese citizenship does not automatically erase existing tax liabilities though.
Individuals could remain liable for taxes on historical gains, depending on how their wealth was structured, even after giving up their nationality, but a genuine change in citizenship and residency could affect future obligations, experts said.
For many wealthy Chinese, relinquishing their nationality remains a significant sacrifice, particularly for those whose businesses and fortunes are tied to the mainland.
Lin said those most willing to take that step generally have few remaining business links to China, with much of their wealth and operations already based offshore.
So where are they looking to move?
For wealthy Chinese seeking an alternative passport rather than merely overseas residency, the Caribbean has emerged as a popular choice.
Countries such as Antigua and Barbuda offer citizenship-by-investment programs that allow eligible applicants to obtain nationality through qualifying investments or contributions.
Tibrewal said Caribbean citizenship can potentially be secured within six months, making it considerably faster than pathways in Europe or the United States, where residency requirements often precede naturalization.
Arton said the appeal is less about permanently relocating and more about greater flexibility to travel and establish an international base.
Global Citizen Solutions said the Caribbean recorded the strongest growth in Chinese inquiries among the destinations it tracked this year.
European countries are also attracting interest, although many offer residency pathways rather than immediate citizenship.
"For Chinese HNWIs who are not willing to give up their citizenship, a portfolio of residencies or long-term visas is a more appealing option," Arton said.
Portugal remains popular through its golden visa program, which offers residency through qualifying investments and a potential longer-term route to citizenship.
Arton also added that Italy is attracting wealthy families through its favorable tax arrangements for qualifying new residents, international schools and financial services infrastructure.
Hungary is another emerging destination, offering long-term residency through qualifying investments starting at 250,000 euros ($290,000).
“Hungary is the one that surprises people,” according to Global Citizen Solutions. “As the larger European golden visa routes have closed or become more expensive, Hungary offers residency in the Schengen area through a regulated fund investment.”
Singapore remains attractive to wealthy Chinese because of its political stability, established wealth management industry, international schools and proximity to mainland China.
Some families are pursuing Singapore permanent residency as part of longer-term citizenship plans, although naturalization is neither automatic nor guaranteed.
Tibrewal said his firm was assisting some clients with plans involving Caribbean citizenship and Singapore residency, with Singapore citizenship a possible longer-term objective.
Australia is another popular option, particularly for families prioritizing education and quality of life.
Malaysia is also gaining attention, especially Kuala Lumpur and Penang, where lower living costs, Chinese-speaking communities and international schools appeal to families, said the migration consultancies.
"We also see interest beyond the obvious hubs in Asia, including Penang and Thailand's long-term resident visa, from families who value lifestyle and lower costs," said Global Citizen Solutions.
Meanwhile, Argentina and parts of Eastern Europe are emerging as alternative destinations for those seeking to diversify their international residency options.
Arton Capital identified Argentina as a market worth watching, while Savory & Partners highlighted growing interest in Serbia, North Macedonia and Bulgaria.
Advisors caution that interest in overseas citizenship does not necessarily translate into completed renunciations or physical relocations.
"It's important to recognize that exploring overseas residency, building a passport portfolio, and relocating an entire family are very different decisions," Arton said.

articles.title_orig: Australia returns ancient stone heads to China after more than 30 years
articles.title_zh: Australia returns ancient stone heads to China after more than 30 years
articles.content_orig:
The Song dynasty sculptures were given to the National Gallery of Australia in the 1990s, a time when art theft was rife in China
Australia has returned two stone sculptures to China after more than 30 years abroad.
The statues, showing the heads of a military official and civil servant, had been given to the National Gallery of Australia in Canberra by a private collector and date back to the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127).
China’s National Cultural Heritage Administration received the heads on Wednesday, according to the state broadcaster CCTV.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft earnings live: Microsoft beats Q1 expectations on top and bottom line on AI growth
articles.title_zh: Microsoft earnings live: Microsoft beats Q1 expectations on top and bottom line on AI growth
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.
Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement , with Azure now its biggest single business.
The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported  $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.
With respect to guidance, Microsoft called for $96 billion to $97.1 billion in fiscal second-quarter revenue, which works out to 18.8% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $95.60 billion in revenue.
For Azure, Hood said she anticipates 49% to 50% growth at constant currency for the fiscal second quarter, compared with the 45.1% StreetAccount consensus.
"We still have demand that exceeds supply," she said.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases. "Some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed," the company's finance chief, Amy Hood, said on a conference call with analysts.
Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft's prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue.
Hood said the company is aiming at over $50 billion in fiscal second-quarter capital expenditures and finance leases, above the StreetAccount consensus of $53.10 billion, with $170 billion for all of calendar 2027 because of the capacity issues.
"In the second half of the fiscal year, we currently expect capex spend to accelerate primarily from CPUs, inclusive of higher memory and storage costs, and GPUs, as well as the 3P capacity deliveries that shifted to H2," she said. The delays have to do with GPU-as-a-service providers, she said.
Free cash flow for the fiscal first quarter declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time.
Microsoft will continue to generate free cash flow through the 2027 fiscal year, but the company will access additional sources of funding when it's attractive to do so, Hood said.
"We're fortunate to have access in the debt markets, given where our rates ratings are, and sort of we haven't been able to — we haven't yet, I would say, tapped that," she said. "And then, of course, there's other options."
Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI.
For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter, despite the delays from third-party providers.
Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.  For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services.
The number of people using the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant is up 50% from last quarter, CEO Satya Nadella said on the call. The company did not disclose the number of paid seats. The recently announced high-end Microsoft 365 E7 productivity bundle now has millions of seats, Hood said.
Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers.
Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand.
As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs , and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration will allow pharmacies to make popular peptides
articles.title_zh: Trump administration will allow pharmacies to make popular peptides
articles.content_orig:
Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has supported broader access to peptides. A new policy will make it easier for small compounding pharmacies to make them. Heather Diehl/Getty Images hide caption
Unproven but popular peptides touted for wellness have been available on the gray market, despite an official ban. Now, the Department of Health and Human Services is looking to bring them out of the shadows.
HHS said in a new policy that it will exercise enforcement discretion for a half dozen peptides, essentially looking the other way when they're made by small compounding pharmacies.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been a vocal supporter of peptides , saying he has used some of them himself.
Peptides are strings of amino acids, shorter than proteins, that can exert powerful effects in the body. Some occur naturally and others are synthetic variations. Wellness influencers and some clinicians have promoted unproven peptides for a wide range of uses, though the evidence for their safety and effectiveness is sparse.
So even though these peptides have not been through the Food and Drug Administration's rigorous drug review and approval process, they could become easier to get. But the policy's focus on smaller producers may mean that pharmacists will have a tough time meeting demand.
In July, a panel of advisers to the FDA voted in favor of expanded access to six peptides through compounding pharmacies. However, at the same meeting the FDA's own scientists recommended against unwinding the existing restrictions on them.
The new policy says compounding is a safer alternative to illicit "research-use-only" peptides that are available online. They're often sourced from sketchy suppliers overseas.
The peptides, and some of their unproven uses, are:
Joshua Fritzler, the president of Olympia and Wesley Pharmaceuticals in central Florida, says people have been asking about these peptides for years. But because they were illegal to compound, his company didn't make them.
The new policy doesn't change their legal status, but it does create a path for small compounders, called 503A compounding pharmacies. It doesn't apply to the larger ones, called 503Bs, that are outsourcing facilities producing higher volumes of medicines.
So at Fritzler's company, only its smaller compounding facility will be able to make the peptides – and only in small quantities, he says.
And that has implications for consumers.
"We won't be able to meet demand," he says, explaining that Olympia will likely only compound one of the six peptides and needs to get its facility ready first. "I don't think all the [503]As in the country could meet the demand."
The Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding's CEO Scott Brunner wrote in a statement that his group is pleased with the administration's decision to allow the peptides to be compounded because it offers a "more accountable alternative" for patients seeking gray market peptides.
"It also brings patients into a system where pharmacy standards, regulatory oversight, and serious adverse event reporting apply," he says.
Brunner warned, however, that it may take some time for compounding pharmacies to begin dispensing these products to patients. That's because ingredient suppliers need to make sure their active ingredients meet the policy's requirements — and pharmacies need to verify that, too.
Several consumer advocacy groups say the policy puts patients at risk, however. The nonprofit Public Citizen noted that Kennedy seems to have acted unilaterally rather than through the typical rulemaking process.
"By allowing unproven and potentially unsafe peptides to be manufactured, marketed and prescribed without concern about potential federal enforcement actions, Kennedy has undermined the FDA and threatened public health," Dr. Robert Steinbrook, Health Research Group Director at Public Citizen wrote in a statement. "All peptide substances should go through the standard FDA approval process for new drugs. The HHS Secretary should support, not sabotage, needed FDA enforcement actions to protect consumers."
Steinbrook advised clinicians to talk to their patients and tell them about the risk of contamination and other adverse effects.
The Partnership for Safe Medicines, which includes various pharmacy and pharmacist organizations around the country, filed a citizen petition last week, urging the FDA to ignore the recommendation from its advisory committee in July to allow compounding pharmacies to make the six peptides.
"Today's decision leaves Americans in a grey area as to whether peptides are safe or not, even though the FDA's own scientists recommended against voting in favor of these substances due to concerns with evidence," its executive director Shabbir Safda wrote in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Spain train crash kills at least 68 as witnesses describe devastating scenes
articles.title_zh: Spain train crash kills at least 68 as witnesses describe devastating scenes
articles.content_orig:
The force of the crash saw several carriage fall down an embankment
A high-speed train crash has killed at least 68 people and injured dozens more in central Spain.
It occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into another train - which was stationary on the tracks - on Wednesday morning. The force saw several carriages fall down an embankment.
The transport minister said a computer failure followed by human error caused the crash, which is one of the worst in Europe's modern history, and Spain's deadliest train disaster in 13 years.
Survivors described harrowing scenes of passengers being thrown into the air, trapped in the wreckage and smashing windows to get out.
The crash happened just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) around 140km (87 miles) south of Madrid, between the municipalities of Mora and Orgaz.
The stationary train, run by private rail operator Iryo, had 147 passengers on board, and had stopped on the tracks because of a computer failure, Spain's Transport Minister Ãscar Puente said.
He explained that when there is a system failure, a 24-hour control centre in Madrid takes over, but it had made an "inexplicable" decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by another train, run by Spain's state-owned railway company, Renfe, which was carrying 397 passengers.
The force of the crash was "brutal", said 62-year-old passenger Salvador Arriza who was sitting in the Renfe-operated train.
Passengers started breaking the windows to get out, he told Reuters, adding that "some people couldn't move because they were trapped amongst the seats."
One of the carriages caught fire, and passengers described devastating scenes of trapped people crying and bleeding, with some buried under debris.
Pictures show that a long piece of railway track had speared through one of the carriages.
Some passengers said the piece of train track that speared through a carriage may have slowed the train down
Tangui Binier, 22, was on the Iryo train and told the BBC that "suitcases started flying and people were screaming" when the train finally came to a halt.
There was a lot of smoke and confusion, he said, and described seeing the train "completely flipped over" when he stepped outside.
"It was hard to witness", Binier said, adding that his father carried a girl who had a broken hip out of the wreckage.
He also described seeing dead bodies and missing limbs: "I don't know if I'll ever recover."
Watch: 'Chaotic scenes' at site of Spain's deadly train crash
Spanish journalist Antonio JimÃ©nez Barca, who works for El Pais newspaper, was walking to the Renfe train's cafeteria when the crash happened.
"I felt like I was being pushed from behind, like I was being thrown to the ground," he described.
"I hit my head horribly... I was covered in blood. There were people on top of me. One person had an injured arm, and another had a head injury."
Another passenger, 46-year-old SebastiÃ¡n Herrero, told El Mundo newspaper that he saw "many people with broken noses, broken arms."
"It was a terrible, terrible impact," he said, adding that he was "in the air for about four or five seconds," which felt like a lifetime.
Many of the passengers said they were in shock, and one sobbed during an interview with a local television station as he described a woman dying in his arms.
"She was very cold and she was all alone," he said, to which the show's presenter also started to cry.
Dozens of ambulances rushed to the scene, and a helicopter evacuated those with the most serious injuries.
Spain's Civil Guard said it would need DNA samples from relatives to identify some victims.
"The whole of Spain is grieving", Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez said during a visit to the crash site. "Lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart, the pain is immense."
Spain was already reeling from a high-speed rail disaster near CÃ³rdoba in January that killed 46 people. It happened on the same rail line, but much further south.
Wednesday's crash is the worst the country has seen since 2013, when when 80 people died on the outskirts of Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain.
"Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure," said Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o, leader of the the main opposition People's Party.
Spanish trade union CSIF has demanded the transport minister resign, accusing him of "scapegoating" a traffic manager, by blaming human error in the control room, instead of "taking responsibility".
SÃ¡nchez and other Spanish politicians cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday, including campaigning for next month's parliamentary elections.
The prime minister said it was "unacceptable" for Spain to have two serious train crashes in one year, and vowed to "get to the bottom of this" and determine if there was any negligence.
"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."

articles.title_orig: Girl seriously injured in wolf attack at German wildlife park
articles.title_zh: Girl seriously injured in wolf attack at German wildlife park
articles.content_orig:
The park keeps Arctic wolves, like those pictured, and grey wolves (file image)
An eight-year-old girl has been seriously injured in a wolf attack at a German wildlife park.
She was inside an enclosure at the JohannismÃ¼hle park in Brandenburg, south of Berlin, with a staff member and two other children when the attack happened, police said.
They said in a statement that the "precise circumstances of the incident are the subject of an ongoing police investigation".
The girl was taken to hospital by helicopter after the incident on Wednesday. No one else was injured.
The park, in the town of Baruth/Mark, has been closed temporarily and is set to reopen on 2 November, according to its website, which did not give further details.
The park keeps grey and arctic wolves, along with other animals including the brown bear and lynx.
The girl was injured by at least one animal and suffered head injuries, according to German newspaper Bild.
It reported that the incident happened before the park opened at 10:00 local time (09:00 GMT) and that the girl could have been taking part in a special visit.
JohannismÃ¼hle offers small group tours to allow visitors to spend time with some animals, with its site mentioning feeding wolves or petting a llama.
The incident comes after a number of other animal attacks at zoos and wildlife parks in Europe.
A keeper at a Dutch zoo died this week after being mauled by a leopard, and a man was killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park earlier this month.

articles.title_orig: King Charles shows off dance moves on second day of Caribbean tour
articles.title_zh: King Charles shows off dance moves on second day of Caribbean tour
articles.content_orig:
King addresses 'suffering and injustices' in Bahamas past
King Charles III has begun his tour of the Caribbean by acknowledging the "great suffering of the past" as he faced calls for slavery reparations.
Speaking an event in the Bahamas celebrating local youth, the King said the country's culture was "born out of darkness", and it was "only right" to acknowledge historic injustices.
His nine-day tour will culminate in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), where the King has confirmed leaders will discuss the region's legacy of slavery.
The visit, his first as monarch, comes in the wake of renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit.
Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during his visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.
Upon his arrival on Tuesday, the King met Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward Davis, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour.
King Charles, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended  independence celebrations for the Bahamas as Prince of Wales in 1973.
The young people in the crowd had been given time off school for the event. "It's my first time seeing him in person out of TikTok so he's out there, it's cool," one student told the BBC.
A small group of protesters gathered close to the rally shouting "pay us what you owe us" and "return artefacts you've stolen."
The group of around a dozen protesters was kept outside the main venue as they called on the King to help change the UK government's position on apologising and offering reparations.
"He's a man of influence. The Crown still has influence. And if they do not do it then we will become a republic and we will turn our backs on England if you do not show respect to the former colonies," said one protester, Sharon Purcer-Cooper.
The King spoke with young people as he attended his first engagement of the trip
The King spoke to these performers at a Nassau rally where the focus was on youth
The King spoke with Philip Edward Davis, Prime Minister of the Bahamas
During his speech in Nassau, the King acknowledged his 50-year-long commitment to fighting climate change and highlighted the challenges faced by low-lying Caribbean islands, saying that "our world cries out for healing".
He went on to call on young people at the rally to "take up the sacred task to play your part" as "in years to come, this will be surely be the measure of every person - how they answered the call to care for planet earth - the source of our life, our prosperity and our security".
The King resumes engagements in the Bahamas on Wednesday, where he will hear how vulnerable the low lying islands of the Caribbean are to climate change.
He will also learn more about the Bahamian tradition of Junkanoo - a cultural festival and street parade.
Buckingham Palace said opportunities for the King to reflect on the legacy of the slave trade will be built into the schedule of his nine-day tour of three Caribbean countries with visits planned to memorials and other places of reflection and remembrance.
A spokesperson for the palace told the BBC that the King's programme on the tour "will primarily focus on shining a light on the many modern partnerships and opportunities for the future", specifically those which are "having a transformative effect on the region".
For the King, the spokesperson added, the "tour is both a new journey but also the continuance of a lifelong one, in which he has sought to engage, understand and educate about the most shameful aspects of our past".
Those themes will be reflected by the King through the nine-day visit, the palace said.
The visit has been planned alongside the governments of the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda with an emphasis on honouring the past but also looking forward to the ambition and possibility for future generations.
The King will move to Guyana later this week where his engagements will focus on the environment and biodiversity.
He will then visit Antigua and Barbuda, where he will be joined by Queen Camilla, for the CHOGM and his keynote speech as leader of the Commonwealth.
The biennial summit will bring together leaders of 56 Commonwealth countries to address shared challenges and advance cooperation.

articles.title_orig: All 16 D&D World of Warcraft Species Revealed
articles.title_zh: All 16 D&D World of Warcraft Species Revealed
articles.content_orig:
As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.
Over the past twenty years, the World of Warcraft MMORPG has introduced dozens of playable species. Now, many of these unique creatures and cultures are making the leap from the desktop to the tabletop courtesy of the upcoming D&D WoW crossover.
In total there are 16 new D&D WoW species. Five of these (Dwarf, Elf, Goblin, Human and Orc) are adaptations of existing D&D 5.5E species, while 11 of them (Dracthyr, Draenei, Earthen, Forsaken, Gnome, Haranir, Pandaren, Tauren, Troll, Vulpera and Worgen) are completely native to the world of Azeroth and appearing in 5.5E for the first time.
To help make sense of it all, we’ve put together this detailed species guide, which includes a high-level explanation of what the species is all about, along with their key traits within the D&D 5.5E ruleset. One important thing to note is that we have also included notes on Renown , which is an optional rule in the 2024 Dungeon Master’s Guide but is a major part of the new D&D Warcraft supplement. Each species has a base Renown score that determines how you interact with Azeroth’s many factions and offers in-game benefits such as access to magic items, discounts on equipment and new Bastion facilities.
With that in mind, below is a complete breakdown of all 16 species from the D&D WoW supplement. You can check them out for yourself, when the book arrives at your local game store, D&D Beyond and Amazon.
Dracthyr are draconic humanoids (somewhat similar to D&D’s Dragonborn ) who were created thousands of years ago by Neltharion , a god-like demon-dragon and leader of the black dragonflight (one of Azeroth’s five great families of dragons, each of which is tasked with protecting one particular aspect of the world). Neltharion combined the power of dragons with the adaptability of the mortal races to create what he believed would be an army of elite soldiers. Unfortunately, Neltharion was corrupted and driven mad by the Old Gods and became the villainous being known as Deathwing. As a result, his army off dracthyr was sealed away in stasis, sleeping for ten thousand years until they were eventually awakened in the Dragon Isles.
In their natural form, dracthyr are winged, scaled warriors, but can transform into a humanoid form known as a visage. In the World of Warcraft MMORPG, dracthyr are the only species that can play the Evoker class (a mechanic that has carried over into the new D&D supplement). It’s also important to note that within the 5.5E rules, a dracthyr’s creature type is Dragon rather than Humanoid, which does matter when it comes to certain spells, abilities and magic items.
Dracthyr are organized into military divisions called weyrns . When you create a dracthyr, you choose which weyrn you belong to. There are five options in the new D&D WoW supplement:
If you choose the Dark Talons (Horde) or the Obsidian Warders (Alliance), your Renown Score with that faction begins at 3. If you choose any other weyrn, your Renown Score with the Valdrakken Accord (the alliance of dragonflights based in the city of Valdrakken) begins at 3.
As a Dracthyr, you have these special traits.
Draenei are tall, blue-skinned humanoids with hooves, tails and face tendrils, and are one of the few playable species not originally from Azeroth. Instead, they are the descendants of a species known as the Eredar, who once dwelled on the distant world of Argus. When the dark Titan Sargeras offered the Eredar unimaginable power, two of their leaders accepted and became unholy lords of the demonic horde known as the Burning Legion . The third leader, the prophet Velen, foresaw these dark events and fled from Argus with his followers, with the group guided by benevolent beings made of holy energy known as naaru .
The Eredar who travelled with Argus called themselves draenei (which meant “exiled ones” in their language) and spent thousands of years fleeing across the cosmos with the Burning Legion in pursuit. Eventually their dimensional ship, known as the Exodar, crash-landed on Azeroth, where they joined the Alliance.
When you create a Draenei, you choose one of four Eredar Lineages:
If you choose the Draenei or Lightforged lineage, your Renown Score with the Exodar (Alliance) begins at 3. Otherwise, you have no starting Renown Score.
As a Draenei, you have these special traits.
At first glance, Azeroth’s Dwarves will feel familiar to most D&D players and fans of fantasy fiction. They’re stout, stubborn and famous for their mining, stonework, engineering and love of weapons and good ale. Their origin, however, is unique to Warcraft. Dwarves descend from the Earthen, beings of living stone built by the Titans (the godlike cosmic beings who shaped Azeroth). When the Old God Yogg-Saron afflicted the earthen with the “curse of flesh,” many asked to be sealed away in hibernation until a cure could be found. Ages later, they awoke as flesh-and-blood dwarves, journeyed to the snowy mountains of Dun Morogh and carved out the great city of Ironforge.
For more than two thousand years, Ironforge prospered through trade with the human kingdoms to the north. Then, about two centuries before the orcs invaded Azeroth, tensions between its three most powerful clans erupted into a civil conflict called the War of the Three Hammers. The Bronzebeard clan won the war and drove its rivals out of the mountain. Today, those old wounds have largely healed, and Ironforge is governed by the Council of Three Hammers, which includes representatives from all three clans and is considered a founding pillar of the Alliance.
When you create a dwarf, you can choose which clan you hail from. There are four options:
Whichever clan you choose, your Renown Score with Ironforge (Alliance) begins at 3.
You have the Dwarf species traits from the 2024 Player’s Handbook.
As a Dwarf, you have these special traits.
Earthen are beings of living stone created eons ago by the god-like Titans using a great machine called the Forge of Wills and were designed to mine and carve out Azeroth’s caverns. Over time, many earthen fell victim to the “curse of flesh,” which was engineered by the Old God Yogg-Saron. These victims became the ancestors of today’s dwarves. Large populations of stone earthen survived, however, primarily on the continent of Khaz Algar, where a titan device called the Awakening Machine roused them from stasis. After the dwarf king Magni Bronzebeard restored the machine, newly awakened earthen were allowed to choose their own path rather than follow the titans’ ancient instructions, and many have since joined the Alliance or the Horde.
In appearance, earthen resemble stocky dwarves carved from stone and infused with Azerite, the crystallized lifeblood of Azeroth. Crystals jut from their bodies and mineral growths take the place of hair and beards. They don’t need to eat, but consuming certain minerals or precious stones can slightly alter their appearance.
As newly awakened free agents with no long-standing ties to either faction, Earthen have no starting Renown Score.
As an Earthen, you have these special traits.
Every Elf of Azeroth traces their roots to the night elves, who once ruled a world-spanning empire built around a lake of raw magical energy known as the Well of Eternity. Their rulers soon became obsessed with arcane magic, which drew the attention of the Burning Legion . The resulting War of the Ancients ended with the Great Sundering, a cataclysm that shattered Azeroth’s single continent into the landmasses that exist today. Ten thousand years of conflict have since splintered elven society into several distinct peoples, five of which are playable in the new D&D 5.5E supplement:
Your starting Renown Score depends on which elven people you hail from:
You have the Elf species traits from the 2024 Player’s Handbook. However, instead of choosing a Drow, High Elf or Wood Elf lineage, you choose one of the four Azeroth Elven Lineages in the table below. (High elv

articles.title_orig: Cruise line folds over fuel costs, booting passengers in Cambodia
articles.title_zh: Cruise line folds over fuel costs, booting passengers in Cambodia
articles.content_orig:
A residential cruise ship halted operations in Cambodia on Tuesday amid soaring fuel costs , leaving passengers in limbo after the U.S. company that operates it ordered them to disembark.
Florida-based Villa Vie Residences said in a news release that it was working to identify “temporary living arrangements” for people aboard The Odyssey, a 642-foot cruise ship that launched from Belfast, Northern Ireland, three years ago and promised passengers “an unparalleled lifestyle of luxury and exploration” as it toured the planet.
Cabins on The Odyssey were for sale or rent.
According to the company , the ship can accommodate 650 residents. A Cambodian official said Wednesday there were 203 passengers and 156 ​crew members on the ship. Some passengers had already departed on ​flights, while others were waiting in the port city of Sihanoukville, Long Dimanche, deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk Province, told media.
The ship is scheduled to refuel before leaving ‌Cambodia on ⁠Saturday, he added.
An executive with the company, Mikael Petterson, declined to provide additional details in an email to NBC News. In a release this year announcing the company’s second residential cruise ship, Petterson said The Odyssey was 85% sold.
The company said in Tuesday’s release that it had taken significant measures to reduce fuel consumption but that those steps had failed to offset the spike in costs.
Global oil prices have surged since the war with Iran began this year, disrupting the world’s flow of fuel. In recent days, oil prices have climbed to their highest levels in months.
“Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution,” the company said. “Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees while we work toward restructuring and recapitalization over the next 60 days. That work is ongoing, and no outcome is assured.”
Randy Cassingham, a resident on the boat, wrote in a blog post that he learned his journey was over after a company official posted a note on a message board for the ship shortly after 7 a.m. Monday.
The Odyssey was entering a “temporary lay up” period — indicating it would no longer be used — and everyone had to disembark by 2 p.m., the message said, according to Cassingham, who runs ResidentialCruising.com and didn’t immediately reply to an interview request.
Cassingham attributed the development to a “cascade of problems” that he would detail later.
Pamela Reckamp, who rented a cabin with her husband and disembarked this month, said in an interview that she wasn’t surprised that the ship’s journey was over.
Reckamp, 59, recalled having attended a meeting in early September at which a company official asked cabin owners to help them raise $1 million so they could leave Ha Long Bay, Vietnam.
“She said, ‘If we don’t get this money, we have about four days of the ship running,’” Reckamp recalled. “‘Then the lights will go off and the AC will go off.’”
When the ship’s financial issues were raised during another meeting a few weeks later, Reckamp recalled, a woman stood up and said she’d bought a cabin in August and hadn’t been made aware of the issues.
“I sold my house,” Reckamp recalled the woman saying. “I sold my car. I bought my home on this ship.”
Residential cruise ship halts operations over fuel costs
Reckamp said she felt terrible for the residents and the staff, who she said were lovely.
“We dodged a bullet,” she added.
Villa Vie Residences didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday night.
In a lawsuit filed last year, a company that bought a cabin on The Odyssey for $469,000 accused Villa Vie Residences of fraud, alleging it misrepresented its financial stability.
The company’s business model was not financially sound, the suit alleges, “but rather precarious.”
The plaintiffs are asking for a jury trial and unspecified damages of more than $100,000. Villa Vie Residences denied the allegations in the suit, which is ongoing.
Other cabins on the ship were available for significantly less money. Even though 85% of the ship was sold, the company said in 2024, prospective residents could still “secure their dream home starting at just $119,000.”
“When we launched Odyssey, we set out to prove that residential cruising wasn’t just possible — it was sustainable,” Petterson said in July.
Tim Stelloh is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Election polls in New Zealand continue to show no clear outcome
articles.title_zh: Election polls in New Zealand continue to show no clear outcome
articles.content_orig:
RNZ / News / Politics / Election 2026
Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2211552%2Fnational-party-mps-feeling-the-pressure-of-party-vote-plunge
Audio player for " Political editor Jo Moir discusses latest RNZ poll " removed for printing
Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2211552%2Fnational-party-mps-feeling-the-pressure-of-party-vote-plunge
Analysis - National is in a fight to save the furniture just nine days out from the polls closing.
The latest RNZ-Reid Research poll has the governing party falling below the 25 percent mark - collecting just 24.8 points as it nears the home stretch to 7 November.
That result is a drop on the 25.9 points it registered in our poll three weeks ago, and even worse than the 25.6 percent National got in the dire 2020 election result.
This poll puts an almost six-point gap between National and Labour, which registered 30.6 percent.
While National is in real danger territory, its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First are sitting on 10.1 and 9.9 respectively, putting the gap between their combined vote and National's at less than five percent.
In a sign the strategic voting phenomenon being pitched by some on the centre-right could be resonating, ACT is up 1.1 - a direct swap with National, which is down by the exact same number.
The strategy is built on the idea that voters on the right give their candidate vote to National and their party vote to ACT or New Zealand First, which has the effect of creating an overhang with National winning more electorate seats than its allocated party vote proportion.
It's a play that has National Party list MPs and those in marginal seats, who are relying on a strong party vote, pulling their hair out as they look at poll after poll with their chances of getting into Parliament diminishing.
Look no further than Paul Goldsmith who has resorted to sending out letters in his electorate asking Epsom voters to "do things differently" and give him the electorate vote as "David Seymour is guaranteed to be re-elected on the ACT Party list".
Adding it would be the "greatest honour" of his career to be the MP for Epsom. Not only that, on RNZ's poll numbers it's the only way he'll be an MP with his list spot of sixth far from safe.
Deputy leader Nicola Willis, senior MP and minister Chris Bishop, and Speaker Gerry Brownlee are in similarily precarious positions and there's two places to point the finger.
Audio player for " Giles Dexter reports in latest RNZ poll results " removed for printing
Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2211552%2Fnational-party-mps-feeling-the-pressure-of-party-vote-plunge
One is a global trend of major parties' falling support in democracies abroad, and political fragmentation leading to previously minor parties growing in support.
That trend has seen the purple vote - the combined Labour and National vote - drop steadily across the course of the year and down to just 55.4 percent in this poll.
The other contributor to National's woes is the Christopher Luxon-shaped hole in its polling.
It takes a likeable leader to keep polling at a level that sees its most senior MPs and current Cabinet ministers return after just three years in power.
After continually choosing to put its electoral success in the hands of Luxon the caucus in some respects has only itself to blame.
Twice there have been confidence votes called on Luxon's leadership and twice he's stared his detractors down and stayed in the job despite eye-wateringly low net approval ratings.
Luxon's net approval score is unchanged in this poll, but that's not a celebration when it's a result of -23.7.
Choosing twice to recommit to Luxon has almost certainly hurt the party vote.
At the same time Luxon's approval is down the drain, Labour leader Chris Hipkins has turned his negative scores of the past two RNZ-Reid Research polls into a positive 5 percent.
That's backed up with him being ahead in the preferred prime minister stakes on 23 percent to Luxon's 17.
While National will be scratching its heads trying to work out how to turn the ship around with just over a week to go, Labour isn't in celebratory land either.
While it's cleared the twenties and hit 30 percent it would still need the Greens and Opportunity to form a government on these numbers.
Likewise with Opportunity holding the balance of power the centre-right bloc would also need Opportunity to get a majority - something Luxon continues to rule out as an option.
With the smaller parties increasing their share of the vote the leverage and influence they'll have in post-election coalition talks also grows.
It makes the promises from National and Labour on the campaign trail meaningless in some respects given the slate will be wiped clean at the negotiating table.
Opportunity looks to have charted a course through the middle putting itself in a strong powerbroker position on 7.2 percent as election day draws closer.
MPs in the coalition government continue to ridicule Opportunity, including National's Erica Stanford who this week called the party a "bunch of flakes" .
Attacks like those lay bare the true extent of the pressure National MPs are coming under.

The cultural venues emerging in China today are quieter, lighter and more deeply rooted than those of recent decades
I served on the Frame Awards 2026 grand jury for the “institutions” categories. Three of the five projects shortlisted for the “cultural space” award were in mainland China: My Museum Beijing, Anji Hood and the Huishan Ancestral Hall Museum in Wuxi. China had 7,046 registered museums at the end of 2024, welcoming 1.49 billion visits that year.
Once a nation has built cultural venues on that scale, the question shifts from how many to what kind. The answers now emerging are quieter, lighter and more deeply rooted than the icons of recent decades.

articles.title_orig: Fed leaves rates steady as governor Lisa Cook dissents
articles.title_zh: Fed leaves rates steady as governor Lisa Cook dissents
articles.content_orig:
The cost of living is Issue No. 1 for voters heading to the polls, but the Federal Reserve saw America’s persistent inflation problem Wednesday and opted not to do anything about it.
At least for the next six weeks, anyway.
Despite consumer prices gaining 3.7% over the past year and the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge stubbornly remaining 50% above the central bank’s target, the decision to hold interest rates steady was widely expected.
That’s because changing rates is a blunt instrument that can inflict serious damage on the economy when ill-timed or used improperly.
“Interest rates get in the cracks,” Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said in a press briefing Wednesday. “They affect everything.”
Central bankers just last month hiked rates for the first time in more than three years, and they want to wait a bit to see how the economy responds before bashing it over the head again with another rate hike.
“Ensuring price stability and watching inflation is not about some fixed date on a calendar or some isolated data point,” Warsh said. “It’s about ensuring we have clear objectives and the right monetary policy.”
Warsh said he was encouraged by the reduction in inflation expectations since the Fed raised rates in September.
By waiting, however, the Fed is also taking a significant gamble. The Fed risks another 2021-like mistake, when it assumed the inflation monster staring the economy directly in the face could be defeated by just ignoring it. (The Fed was disastrously wrong).
This time may truly be different, and not acting with haste could prove prescient.
Or it could force the central bank to give the economy some December shock therapy that it may have been able to avoid with an October rate hike.
Jobs. Hiking rates increases businesses’ borrowing costs, which leaves them with less money to hire.
Now may be a perilous time to mess with the job market: The US economy added only 29,000 jobs in September, well below expectations. And the September report showed that the economy added 60,000 fewer jobs over the previous two months than previously believed.
The labor market is by no means in bad shape, but it has been on shaky ground. The US economy lost 10,000 jobs in July and in seven of the past 16 months. Although unemployment remains at a healthy 4.2%, economists describe the economy as “low hire, low fire.”
In other words, your position may not be at risk, but if you leave your job, you may have trouble finding a new one.
Markets. Treasury yields moved higher since the last Fed rate hike, with bond yields at one point hitting multi-decade highs. Yields have slipped a bit since, returning to where they were in mid-September, but the still relatively high bond yields can help give the Fed cover, because they have an effect similar to the Fed funds rate, slowing the economy and inflation.
The Fed also doesn’t like to surprise investors – even in Warsh’s new keep-‘em-guessing era. The market had priced in a 91% chance that the Fed would hold rates, according to CME’s FedWatch tool, and a hike could have sent the markets into a painful rebalancing.
Timing. The Fed’s decision may also have been influenced, at least somewhat, by the upcoming election. Narayana Kocherlakota, the former Minneapolis Fed president, told my colleague Matt Egan that the Fed hesitated to raise rates Wednesday because it wanted insulation from President Donald Trump’s criticism. But the Fed throughout its history has changed rates many times just as voters were heading to the polls, my colleague Elisabeth Buchwald also noted .
The “transitory” error: The Fed typically doesn’t get involved when supply shocks like the Iran-war-induced energy crisis cause inflation. They’re notoriously temporary, hard to predict and insensitive to rate changes.
But supply shocks sometimes lead to bigger problems that the Fed can help fix. The Fed should know: It just went through this.
As the economy emerged from the pandemic, the Fed made a mistake with inflation, declaring it a result of a “transitory” supply shock related to the Russia-Ukraine war and massive supply chain snarls. It ended up becoming the most significant inflation problem in a generation. The Fed, caught off guard, was forced to raise rates at a historic pace – three consecutive hikes of three-quarters of a percentage point.
Ultimately, the Fed succeeded at lowering out-of-control inflation to more manageable levels, but not before consumer prices peaked at an annual rate of 9.1%, the highest in four decades.
This time may be no different: Inflation is already spilling over into other parts of the economy.
Particularly concerning in the September consumer inflation report was the surprising rebound in housing and rent costs, a significant contributor to inflation that had cooled off in the spring and summer. And the cost of other services rose higher than expected, too – prices that tend to rise (and stay high) as yoga studios, lawn services and the like charge their customers more to make up for their rising costs.
Also driving inflation: Investment in data centers and technology powering AI has propelled the economy into overdrive – and maybe helped overheat it. Prices for electricity, building materials, labor, and personal tech like smartphones and laptops have all risen as a result.
More war? This energy price spike could get worse before it gets better. Trump has strongly hinted (and CNN has reported ) that the United States and Israel could escalate the war with Iran after the midterm elections, potentially sending oil prices higher.
It would be foolhardy for the Fed to make a decision based on a rumor. And energy prices can quickly swing lower. For example, the Trump administration’s announcement of an energy ceasefire in Russia has held surprisingly well, dramatically increasing the amount of diesel Russia produced in the past couple weeks, which could significantly lower global diesel prices – if Ukraine continues to hold off on its drone strikes on Russian refineries.
But the prolonged energy price spike is already raising prices across the economy, and waiting to hike again could place the Fed behind the curve.
Boiling frogs. Rate hikes work with a delayed effect, and sharper rate changes can have deleterious effects on the financial system, markets and the economy. This economic frog tends to stay in the pot when the heat is turned up gradually.
If escalations in the Iran war and Russia-Ukraine war resume, that could force the Fed into a difficult position of hiking rates by even more than expected in its next meeting in December – potentially by a half point, in a kind of make-up call.
The massive, successive rate hikes throughout 2022 sent the stock market into its biggest annual decline since the financial crisis and put the housing market on ice. But the economy didn’t go into a recession – a trick the Fed has rarely pulled off when it hikes rates.
It’s not a wager a lot of economists are eager to place again.

articles.content_orig:
The move comes just days ahead of the US midterm elections, in which the rising cost of living has been a key issue
The US Federal Reserve on Wednesday held interest rates steady, in line with market expectations, days ahead of crucial midterm elections where surging inflation has been a key issue.
The 12-member Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to hold rates at a target range between 3.75 to 4.00 per cent, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation, after having hiked for the first time in three years at its previous meeting in September.
“The accumulation of more information will help the committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the committee’s 2 per cent goal,” the Fed said in a statement announcing its decision.

articles.title_orig: Dutch Zookeeper Dies After Rare Mauling by a Leopard
articles.title_zh: Dutch Zookeeper Dies After Rare Mauling by a Leopard
articles.content_orig:
A zookeeper has died from her injuries days after she was attacked by a leopard at the Dutch safari park where she worked.
The unnamed employee, who had worked at the Beekse Bergen safari park for almost four decades, was attacked by the animal on Saturday and died on Tuesday.
“With enormous sadness, we have to report that the animal caretaker of safari park Beekse Bergen passed away today from the injuries she sustained on Saturday, October 24, in an incident with a leopard in the park,” the park said in a statement Tuesday.
“Her passing also deeply affects us all, and we are intensely grieving with her family, friends and loved ones. We ask for peace and privacy for her loved ones and our staff, so that they can process this profound loss,” the statement added.
The woman suffered serious wounds to her head and neck while working in an enclosure with two male Persian leopards, the Associated Press reported.
The woman contacted colleagues via a walkie talkie after the incident in the leopard’s enclosure and an ambulance and trauma helicopter were dispatched at around 11 a.m. local time Saturday, AP added. She underwent emergency surgery but her condition worsened on Sunday evening.
The employee joined the park, located in the southern Netherlands, when she was 17 years old and had worked there “with short breaks for almost 40 years,” the park’s statement added.
CNN affiliate NOS reported that the zookeeper had been working with the leopards for eight years and had been working alone in the enclosure with two male Persian leopards when she was attacked.
There are no cameras inside the enclosure, the park told NOS, which also reported that the animals have been treated as normal since the incident.
The park said that an independent investigation had been launched into the woman’s death.
Rhino kills zookeeper and seriously injures another in Austria
Home to more than 100 species of animals, Beekse Bergen offers visitors the choice of seeing the safari park by foot, car, bus and boat.
This is not the first time a member of staff at a zoo or safari park has been fatally injured by an animal.
In 2023, a zookeeper was killed in Austria after being attacked by a rhino. The incident, in which another zookeeper was injured, occurred at Salzburg Hellbrunn Zoo. Two years prior to that, a woman working at a safari park in Chile was killed by a tiger while working in the big cats’ enclosure.
CNN’s Rose Roobeek contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: War against Iran won’t distract America from China’s military buildup, Hegseth tells Pacific allies
articles.title_zh: War against Iran won’t distract America from China’s military buildup, Hegseth tells Pacific allies
articles.content_orig:
An Iranian flag is seen as missiles and air defense systems are displayed at Baharestan Square in Tehran, Iran, on September 29, 2026.
President Donald Trump’s conflict with Iran has become a political liability for his administration. Since the last U.S. strikes on Iran fell on Sept. 8, Trump has publicly ruled out attacking Iran before the November midterm elections—and promised to end the conflict after them.
Then, rumblings grew that U.S. and Israeli military planners had reportedly drawn up new strike options against Iran, including the possible use of the largest non-nuclear weapon in the American arsenal: the GBU-43/B, also dubbed “the Mother of All Bombs”.
The targets purportedly would be Iran’s nuclear facilities and energy infrastructure, though there are doubts about whether the bomb could penetrate Iran’s most deeply buried sites. According to these reports, Trump apparently is seeking a strike he could present as a military victory and then end the war without appearing to back down.
But such an approach risks triggering a far wider war than Washington intends. Tehran remains unlikely to let Washington end the conflict quickly and, fearing a potential attack from the U.S., could itself strike first. Either scenario could lead to a new round of fighting far more destructive than the last.
Reports of military plans involving “the mother of all bombs” came against the backdrop of two other worrying developments. First, Iran has been escalating its naval attacks, likely in response to increased flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Notably, two UAE-owned cargo ships, the GFS Pride and the Cape Dao , were struck in the Strait as part of this sharp uptick.
Secondly, diplomatic efforts appear to have hit a wall. In late September, Trump rejected the proposal Tehran had put forward on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly: an end to fighting on all fronts, including Lebanon; the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade and oil sanctions; the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets; and the reopening of Hormuz within seven days. Instead, Washington insists that Iran must take steps regarding its nuclear program as part of the package, something Iranian leaders say they will only do at a later stage.
The timing of any U.S.-Israeli attack remains uncertain. While Trump has said he will not resume attacks before the midterms, Israel held its election on Oct. 27, a week earlier, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had reportedly sought renewed fighting before both elections.
American and Israeli objectives may differ, of course. Trump appears to want something he can portray as a spectacular military victory without having to undergo another prolonged war, while Netanyahu’s rhetoric about “ finishing the job ” suggests more ambitious goals, potentially including toppling the Islamic Republic. Tehran seems to be preparing for either scenario with its own response: a prolonged, region-wide war designed to impose devastating economic costs.
The dominant perspective in Tehran is that the next war must be fought in a way that makes it so costly that a future U.S. president would not contemplate another. Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said in late September that Iran “will not stop until we have driven the United States out of the region, punished the aggressor, and established permanent deterrence so that no one will dare attack Iran.”
That logic, should it prevail, rules out a symbolic, tit-for-tat exchange. In Tehran’s view, a limited American strike on Pickaxe Mountain , the fortified nuclear site near Natanz that Trump has repeatedly evoked, followed by a limited Iranian response, would send Washington precisely the wrong message: that it can attack Iran’s nuclear facilities, register domestic political gain, and pay a limited, acceptable cost. Iranian officials have therefore warned that even a symbolic, non-lethal strike would trigger a broad response, denying Trump the quick exit he may have asked of his war planners.
Under this scenario, Iran would target regional energy and economic infrastructure. “In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one will sell oil,” Ghalibaf has warned . The UAE is particularly exposed: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, has accused it of oil “ smuggling ” in cahoots with U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). Rezaei also identified new potential targets: undersea cables, data centers, and AI infrastructure in the region, which he claims are worth “more than $2 trillion.” Ghalibaf subsequently extended the threat to regional governments and investors, threatening that anyone providing “funding, equity, land, or energy” to AI companies that “facilitate military aggression” against Iran “will face coercive action.”
If raising the cost of war is the first instrument in Iran’s calculus, duration is the second. Ali Balali , an adviser to the IRGC’s Aerospace Force commander, suggested Iran would conserve its arsenal in preparation for a prolonged confrontation, rather than expend it early. Two days later, Iranian Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia argued that the enemy’s weak point is a prolonged war.
Timing is a third dimension in Iranian thinking. Iranian military officials have increasingly mentioned the possibility of striking first, preemptively. Akraminia stated that if Iran were to conclude that an attack by the U.S. and/or Israel is imminent, “we will certainly engage in preemptive warfare.” Mehdi Mohammadi , strategic affairs adviser to Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, went further, arguing that a successful strategy requires not only striking first but also delivering a decisive blow capable of “changing the balance.” There is thus at least the possibility that Iran might move early, and then fight long.
That could occur due to miscalculation resulting from ambiguous American and Israeli signals: leaked strike plans, carrier and amphibious deployments, and aircraft approaching but not entering Iranian airspace. Military experts in Iran see this pattern as an effort to normalize military activity and regain the element of surprise. Tehran could thus mistake military signaling for an imminent attack and strike preemptively, even though it may not want another round of war.
The fourth element concerns the range of those Tehran would hold responsible in the event of an attack. On Oct. 5 Ali Abdollahi , chief of staff of Iran’s armed forces, declared that if the United States acted against Iran “directly or indirectly through Israel,” Iranian forces would retaliate against the United States. The warning carries more weight in the wake of Trump’s decision to openly back Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s election. Indeed, some in Tehran interpreted this as a signal that Washington would allow Israel to strike Iran after the midterms. As a result, Tehran has made clear that even were Israel to carry out the attack on its own, U.S. forces and assets in the region would face retaliation.
This interpretation suggests that the scope of Iran’s response to a U.S. strike likely would be far wider. Its conduct in Hormuz since late September offers a preview of how it could broaden the conflict. When the UAE, backed by CENTCOM, kept oil moving through a southern corridor along the Omani coast, the IRGC shifted its attacks from small shuttle tankers to supertankers and stated that vessels using the “illegal corridor” would be “pursued and interdicted across the region.” Strikes followed off the UAE coast and near Qatar. An escalation in the region could drive Iran to go after vital energy and other infrastructure across the Gulf.
Iran’s regional partners also could widen the conflict, although Tehran does not fully control their actions. In Yemen, the Houthis have already opened a second maritime front in the Red Sea, threatening shipping and increasing pressure on Saudi Arabia. Microsoft shares rose 5% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.

Net income of $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, increased from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, in the same quarter of last year. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million impact from investing in OpenAI.

Microsoft has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to accommodate artificial intelligence demand. The company had $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30%. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.

Analysts polled by StreetAccount had expected $32.32 billion, which would have represented growth of more than 44%. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments for the first time since 1998. For the past 11 years it had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
Agents and Infra gave Microsoft $76.80 billion of its revenue, which was up almost 25% and more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. articles.title_orig: Microsoft cloud revenue beats estimates in sign that AI bet is paying off
articles.title_zh: Microsoft cloud revenue beats estimates in sign that AI bet is paying off
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.
Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement , with Azure now its biggest single business.
The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported  $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.
With respect to guidance, Microsoft called for $96 billion to $97.1 billion in fiscal second-quarter revenue, which works out to 18.8% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $95.60 billion in revenue.
For Azure, Hood said she anticipates 49% to 50% growth at constant currency for the fiscal second quarter, compared with the 45.1% StreetAccount consensus.
"We still have demand that exceeds supply," she said.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases. "Some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed," the company's finance chief, Amy Hood, said on a conference call with analysts.
Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft's prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue.
Hood said the company is aiming at over $50 billion in fiscal second-quarter capital expenditures and finance leases, above the StreetAccount consensus of $53.10 billion, with $170 billion for all of calendar 2027 because of the capacity issues.
"In the second half of the fiscal year, we currently expect capex spend to accelerate primarily from CPUs, inclusive of higher memory and storage costs, and GPUs, as well as the 3P capacity deliveries that shifted to H2," she said.
Free cash flow for the fiscal first quarter declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time.
Microsoft will continue to generate free cash flow through the 2027 fiscal year, but the company will access additional sources of funding when it's attractive to do so, Hood said.
Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI.
For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter, despite the delays from third-party providers.
Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.  For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services.
The number of people using the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant is up 50% from last quarter, CEO Satya Nadella said on the call. The company did not disclose the number of paid seats. The recently announced high-end Microsoft 365 E7 productivity bundle now has millions of seats, Hood said.
Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers.
Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand.
As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs , and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities.
Executives will discuss the results with analysts and issue guidance on a conference call starting at 5:30 p.m. ET.
This story is developing. Please check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: With 90% of votes counted, Netanyahu bloc has 53 seats, Eisenkot’s 48; Arab parties surge to 19
articles.title_zh: With 90% of votes counted, Netanyahu bloc has 53 seats, Eisenkot’s 48; Arab parties surge to 19
articles.content_orig:
The leader of Israel’s Balad party has condemned the country’s main political leaders for refusing to form a coalition with Arab parties, even after a record showing in polls could make them kingmakers for the next parliament after no clear winner emerged.
Sami Abu Shehadeh told Al Jazeera that Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the population, are being treated as illegitimate partners despite their turnout.
“This is racism,” he said. “We are a legitimate elected leadership of the national minority. The vast majority of our people decided that we are their leadership.”
Arab parties are on course to win a record 19 seats, giving them potentially decisive leverage over the main political blocs. With 85 percent of the vote counted, Israel’s Central Elections Committee has Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc ahead with at least 53 seats, and the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot on 48.
Both are short of the 61 needed to govern. Netanyahu says Israelis chose a strong right-wing government, while Eisenkot says they voted for change.
Abu Shehadeh, who leads Balad, one of the Joint List’s three parties, was not a candidate.
Israel’s elections committee voted to disqualify him at the request of far-right Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who accused him of supporting the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack due to an article issued the following day in which Abu Shehadeh called it an “important historical event”.
Abu Shehadeh subsequently told the Supreme Court he did not support “armed struggle” but acknowledged that a paragraph in the article had been incorrectly worded. He said his intention was to call for moving the conflict towards a political process.
He withdrew in October after a majority of the Supreme Court panel appeared willing to approve the disqualification. He rejects the grounds and said the court had made clear that Israel has “two different judicial systems, one for the Jews and one for the Arabs”.
“We are very proud of the Arab Palestinian minority in Israel that went in this very high percentage of voting,” he told Al Jazeera. The community’s first promise to voters, he said, was to prevent “this gang of criminals” from returning to power, naming Netanyahu and far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Ben-Gvir. “So our first promise, we can keep it from now .”
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, said Netanyahu “has scared off everybody from talking to the Palestinian Israeli parties”, leaving him best placed to “call the shots”. She said that Eisenkot and his allies have indicated that they want a Zionist government and “do not want to form a government” with the Arab parties, leaving them few options.
Danny Ayalon, a former Israeli ambassador to the United States, told Al Jazeera that turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel came in “really unprecedented numbers” and that the parties “are going to have some significant clout”.
Mathematically, he said, Eisenkot’s bloc could join forces with the two Arab parties and pass the threshold, though it would take “political wizardry”. Yousef Jabareen, who leads the Joint List, has said his alliance’s “hands are extended” to oust Netanyahu.
Abu Shehadeh set out what Palestinian citizens want from the next government.
“We are against genocide and we are against apartheid. We want to promote a different political alternative, one which is based on the values of freedom, justice and equality for both people who are living between the river and the sea.”
Of Netanyahu, he said: “Our problem … is that he is a war criminal.”
A UN commission said in a report published on Monday that Israel has continued to commit genocide in Gaza after last October’s US-brokered ceasefire in the enclave.
The Hague-based International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in 2024 for war crimes during the Gaza war.
